caseStudy.eyebrow: Repositioning a category for the AI era
caseStudy.context: Workvivo had established itself as an Employee Experience Platform. As enterprise software moved into an AI-native era, the challenge was bigger than adding AI features to the existing story: the company needed a credible new ambition without abandoning the employee-experience equity that made it distinctive.
caseStudy.challenge: What should Workvivo become when AI changes how employees interact with information, systems, and work? A generic ‘we’re now an AI company’ claim would have discarded the adoption, culture, frontline reach, and trust the platform had already earned.
caseStudy.insight: AI becomes more valuable when it lives inside an employee experience people already use. The platform story shifted toward an AI-native headquarters for every employee, captured in the central idea: Give work a home.
contribution: Strategic positioning and category narrative
Messaging architecture across IT, HR, and Comms buyers
Launch strategy, seller narrative, and website story
Analyst story and competitive framing
Portfolio narrative connecting Workvivo HQ to the broader AI strategy
decisions: Position AI as embedded in the employee experience—not bolted on
Make adoption part of the AI ROI story
Frame one destination where employees can understand, find, and increasingly act
Keep frontline employees inside the enterprise AI narrative
caseStudy.outcome: Workvivo publicly launched HQ while serving 9 million users and after surpassing $100M ARR. Those are company proof points during Shauna’s tenure, not outcomes attributed to her alone.
caseStudy.learning: Repositioning works when it expands what a brand can mean without erasing the reason customers trusted it in the first place.

caseStudy.eyebrow: From a manual QA rubric to a buyer-focused decision aid
caseStudy.context: Positioning reviews often produce broad opinions rather than specific, actionable questions. The original AI Positioning QA made a rubric inspectable, but asking reviewers to complete eight dimensions created too much work before they received useful feedback.
caseStudy.challenge: Make the review immediately useful for enterprise IT messaging while retaining traceability. A CIO, an architecture lead and an internal champion can read the same asset with different responsibilities; an awareness asset should not be judged as a procurement brief.
caseStudy.insight: Start with the buyer’s remit and the job of the message. Surface the questions that matter next, show the source passages behind the diagnosis, and leave the claim and publication decision with a human.
contribution: Defined the IT-buyer scope, review experience and evidence standard
Directed AI-assisted prototyping in ChatGPT and implementation in Codex
Shaped six audience lenses, distinct buying roles and stage-aware review guidance
Pressure-tested scoring, source traceability, export behavior and input changes
Integrated the live tool, documentation and visual identity into this portfolio
decisions: Separate awareness stage from purchase stage: what the reader knows differs from what the buying group is deciding
Replace the manual-first interface with Gut Reaction, priority changes and buyer questions
Keep deep review inside the app with matching passages and an editable rewrite brief
Call the score language-signal coverage: it is not buyer readiness, factual verification or market validation
Retain the original eight-dimension evaluator as a separate workflow rather than equating its score with the new six-gate model
architecture: Static HTML and CSS provide the interface; vanilla JavaScript runs locally in the browser
A pure evaluation module contains six IT profiles, three buying roles, purchase-stage weights and language checks
The UI module renders source excerpts, prioritised questions, stage guidance and the rewrite brief
Markdown export preserves the source, context, supplied proof and edited rewrite; the app makes no model or network calls
The portfolio hosts a versioned copy of the public runtime, with a source commit and file hashes recorded in its manifest
tooling: ChatGPT for prototype iteration and Codex for integration, refactoring and checks
Node’s test runner for deterministic scoring and export tests
GitHub for version control and GitHub Pages for static hosting
Generated case-study artwork; interface styling follows the portfolio palette
safeguards: Supplied proof is displayed as unverified context and cannot inflate the score of the source copy
Edits invalidate displayed results and exports; source HTML is escaped rather than executed
Quoted passages preserve the original source whitespace
No automatic saving, tracking or external model calls in the tool
Private research attachments are not published; unsupported research percentages were withheld
validation: 44 automated checks passed at integration, retaining the original evaluator tests
New checks cover proof isolation, exact excerpts, export context and all 54 combinations of remit, buying role and purchase stage
Browser checks covered example review, deep review, edited-brief export, escaped HTML, stale-result invalidation and the 390px mobile layout
Keyword stuffing, negation and irrelevant evidence remain known limitations; independent human calibration and external model benchmarking have not been completed
caseStudy.outcome: A live IT messaging review that gives immediate, inspectable guidance and a reusable rewrite brief. The build demonstrates how positioning judgment can become a practical workflow. It does not establish commercial lift, buyer agreement or production-grade approval governance.
caseStudy.learning: A useful review system must make its limits as visible as its recommendations. Simplifying the interface only helps if the evidence and the human decision remain clear.

caseStudy.eyebrow: Building an AI-enabled PMM operating model
caseStudy.context: AI-first Product Marketing is not simply a team using ChatGPT. Shauna has been exploring how AI can change the operating model of PMM itself—and where human judgment must remain accountable.
caseStudy.challenge: High-value PMM time disappears into retrieval, repeated seller questions, monitoring, synthesis, recurring research, and first-pass analysis. The strategic question is which work requires human judgment and which work can be processed or automated.
caseStudy.insight: AI does more of the processing. PMM remains accountable for the thinking. Retrieval, extraction, monitoring, classification, and repeatable analysis can accelerate; positioning, pricing, claims, category strategy, and executive recommendations still need accountable judgment.
contribution: Seller-facing competitive intelligence and automated monitoring
AI-assisted win/loss analysis and lightweight decision tools
IT Pressure Test
This portfolio and its grounded agent experience
Reusable research, synthesis, and PMM workflows

decisions: Design around workflows rather than collecting tools
Keep a human in the loop for consequential claims and decisions
Encode PMM expertise into evaluation criteria
Use prototypes to learn before deciding whether to build, buy, or stop
caseStudy.outcome: The result is a growing set of practical systems that increase PMM leverage while keeping strategic accountability human. The tools are not the proof; the workflow design and operating choices are.
caseStudy.learning: Technical expertise for a PMM is the ability to understand enough of the system to make better product, pricing, trust, and go-to-market decisions.

caseStudy.eyebrow: Turning a résumé into an evidence-grounded conversation
caseStudy.context: A static portfolio can show the work, but it cannot adapt to the question a recruiter, hiring manager, or technical stakeholder actually wants answered. Shauna designed a live ElevenLabs experience that lets visitors explore her career, case studies, technical builds, and working principles through voice or text. She also created a voice persona from her own voice and gave the agent a defined personality so the experience feels recognisably hers without pretending to be her.
caseStudy.challenge: The agent needed to be persuasive without becoming a hype machine. It had to answer broad career questions quickly, go deep on named projects, distinguish work Shauna built from products she marketed, link back to public evidence, and avoid turning company outcomes or technical fluency into unsupported personal claims.
caseStudy.insight: A credible portfolio agent is a voice, context, workflow, and evaluation problem—not simply a prompt. Better answers came from defining the persona, separating durable rules from retrievable evidence, routing different intents to specialist answer modes, comparing model outputs, and analysing failures where attribution, role fit, or technical ownership could drift.

Engineered the system prompts, answer contract, evidence standard, and guardrails

Built the workflow and intent-routing conditions for technical questions, case-study deep dives, career history, working style, and role-fit pressure tests
Compared outputs from multiple models and analysed response quality, grounding, tone, and failure patterns

Treat live platform configuration and repository evidence as separate states; published files document the design but do not prove every console setting is active

Nine focused knowledge documents are configured for RAG so the agent retrieves only the evidence relevant to the question
A canonical claim ledger separates externally verified facts, public artifacts, self-reported experience, company context, and work still in progress

tooling: ElevenLabs Conversational AI for the agent runtime, custom voice persona, speech interface, workflow, model configuration, and knowledge retrieval

Structured evaluation and qualitative analysis for comparing model outputs and finding recurring failure patterns

validation: Fifteen acceptance questions cover the most common recruiter and technical-review journeys
A 13-question evaluation set tests positioning, technical evidence, ownership boundaries, unsupported claims, role-fit nuance, leadership, and concise voice responses
Multiple model outputs were tested against comparable prompts to evaluate answer quality and trade-offs

caseStudy.outcome: The result is a live, inspectable portfolio interface that demonstrates more than familiarity with AI tools. It shows Shauna's ability to shape a voice persona, engineer prompts, build an intent-routing workflow, configure retrieval and guardrails, compare model behaviour, analyse tests, and translate the technical decisions into a clear professional story. The agent runs on ElevenLabs; Shauna designed, configured, tested, documented, and integrated the experience rather than engineering the underlying voice models or platform runtime.
caseStudy.learning: The quality of an agent is shaped less by the cleverness of one prompt than by the discipline of its context, routing, evidence, evaluation, and boundaries.

caseStudy.context: HQ Agent extended Workvivo beyond communications and employee experience into trusted enterprise answers, search, self-service, and agentic task execution. It sat at the intersection of enterprise knowledge, RAG, permissions, employee experience, and Zoom’s broader AI technology.
caseStudy.challenge: The launch could not be reduced to ‘better enterprise search.’ It needed a clear category, a credible trust story, an understandable relationship with Workvivo HQ and ZoomMate, and sustainable packaging for different levels of AI value.
caseStudy.insight: The most useful commercial progression was SEARCH → ANSWER → ACTION: from finding information, to receiving a grounded answer, to increasingly completing the task. The launch idea became: From search, to answer, to job done.

Seller narrative and enablement

decisions: Market the buyer value of RAG—not the acronym
Use ‘grounded, cited, and permission-aware’ instead of unsafe absolute claims
Differentiate HQ Agent’s employee support from ZoomMate’s deeper productivity use cases
Price levels of AI value rather than charging for novelty
caseStudy.outcome: The result was a portfolio and launch narrative designed to make a technically complex enterprise AI product easier to understand, sell, and evaluate. Shauna shaped the commercial story; she did not engineer the underlying AI system.
caseStudy.learning: Technical depth matters in Product Marketing when it changes the claim, the value, the packaging, or the buyer’s trust.

caseStudy.context: Meta announced the closure of Workplace. Workvivo was named Meta’s only preferred migration partner, creating a major, time-bound market opportunity and a highly visible competitive GTM motion.
caseStudy.challenge: Workvivo had to move quickly while differentiating against competitors, reducing migration risk, addressing customer uncertainty, enabling sellers, and converting a temporary market event into durable commercial opportunity.
caseStudy.insight: The winning story needed to combine urgency with reassurance. Migration could not feel like a technical transfer alone; it needed to feel like a credible path from a closing platform to a stronger long-term employee experience.

caseStudy.context: Workvivo expanded into People Intelligence with Seer, moving into a buyer and category conversation adjacent to its employee-experience strengths.
caseStudy.challenge: Seer could not sound like another survey platform. The story needed to explain how employee feedback moves beyond collection—turning large volumes of qualitative signal into insight that leaders and managers can act on.
caseStudy.insight: The narrative became LISTEN → UNDERSTAND → ACT. The Listening Gap gave the strategy a memorable tension: organisations often collect employee feedback, but struggle to convert what they hear into meaningful action.

Launch strategy
Pricing and packaging
Competitive strategy
Seller narrative and enablement

decisions: Anchor the story in action—not survey collection

caseStudy.outcome: Seer established a people-intelligence expansion story spanning employee listening, AI-assisted insight, manager intelligence, and action. No unverified Seer revenue or adoption metrics are claimed.
caseStudy.learning: Adjacent-market entry becomes credible when the narrative explains both the new capability and why the existing brand has earned the right to compete.
